name: Amira Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Amira, I'm 58, and I buy paper cups, takeaway boxes, napkins and cling film for a food-service distributor on the edge of the city. I'm at my desk by 7:30 with a mug of tea, checking which lines are running low, then I ring or email the factory reps. About half my day is haggling over price and delivery dates, the rest is chasing late trucks and sorting out damaged pallets.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the phone calls. I've known the rep at the cup factory, Brigitte, for twenty years, and she'll warn me before a price rise. What wears me out is the spreadsheet we have to update every afternoon, and the new targets from head office every quarter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, we've heard it all before. Last year the software people told us the system would order everything itself, and I still fix the same mistakes by hand. At the union meeting I'd probably joke that the robot can have the late trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd think it's fine for me, but I'd still be nervous. Head office likes to cut a desk whenever they find a reason, and a bit of time saved is a reason. I'm 58, and I don't fancy being the desk they pick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do now. I'd keep the supplier calls going, maybe ask the union rep to get the job-security wording in writing, and keep putting my 400 a month into savings. I wouldn't touch the new software unless I was told to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it feels like a mild headache, not a storm. I'm calm about the work itself. What bugs me is the rent on my daughter's flat that we help with, and our own cushion is only about four months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep your savings going. What would you do if the savings dipped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop helping my daughter with the flat first, and I'd hate it. Then the holiday we planned for next autumn. My partner Tomas works at the council depot, so we're not on the edge, but four months is not a lot if one of us loses hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said head office might cut a desk. Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Poor Dariusz, he's 61 and does our invoice matching. If a program matches invoices cheaper, he's gone before I am. I'd go and sit with him and ask the union what we could ask for, like early-leaver pay.

say: I'd say we've **heard it before**, and the system still needs me to fix its mistakes.
At the union meeting I'd joke that the robot is welcome to the **late trucks**.
think: I'm fine for now, but a little time saved gives head office a **reason to cut** a desk.
At 58, I don't want to be the **desk they pick**.
do: Keep ringing suppliers and **carry on** as I do today.
Ask the union rep to get **job-security wording** in writing.
Keep putting **400 a month** into savings.
feel: Mostly calm about the work, with a **steady background worry** about money and my daughter's rent.
S0.quote: Last year the software people told us the system would order everything itself, and I still fix the same mistakes by hand.
fieldNote: Resistant to new tools, so she treats hype with open **scorn** but is privately wary of cuts.
Already carries money pressure: helps her daughter with rent and has about four months saved.
Looks to the union first, a clear marker of her progressive outlook.

steps.text: Keep ringing the cup and packaging reps every morning
Put 400 a month into savings as usual
Ask the union rep for job-security wording in writing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not fair that buying, checking and booking are the very jobs they name. That's my whole desk. I'd tell the union we need rules before they roll anything out, and tell my friends not to be fooled that it only hits young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in the line of fire. Ordering, checking invoices, chasing stock, that's most of what I do apart from the haggling. If software does the spreadsheet bit, head office will ask why they need three buyers, and I'm the oldest and the slowest with new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a no-forced-redundancy deal. I'd try the ordering tool once with a younger colleague next to me, and I'd talk to Tomas about whether I could stop at 62 instead of 65. I'd also stop the extra 150 a month we give my daughter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing at the edge of a pool in winter. I know I have to get in, and I'm cross that nobody asked me. Mostly I'd be anxious and a bit ashamed that I never learned the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd try the ordering tool with a younger colleague. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Mia from the next desk, she's 29 and not shy. I'd ask her to sit with me for half an hour on a Friday afternoon, when it's quiet, and I'd write the steps in my notebook. I'd hate every minute but I'd do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for this kind of change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big retail chains and the investors behind them. They push prices down, then buy software so nobody argues back. I don't blame the software, I blame the people who decide who gets the saving.

say: I'd say **buying, checking and booking** are my whole desk, so this isn't only a young person's problem.
I'd tell the union we need **rules** before anything rolls out.
think: Privately, I think I'm in the **line of fire**, and I'm the slowest with new tools.
If software does my spreadsheet, head office will ask why they need **three buyers**.
do: Push the union for a **no-forced-redundancy** deal.
Try the ordering tool once with **Mia (29)** beside me.
Stop the extra **150 a month** to my daughter and talk to Tomas about stopping at 62.
feel: Anxious, and **cross** that nobody asked me, with some shame that I never learned the tools.
S1.quote: I don't blame the software, I blame the people who decide who gets the saving.
fieldNote: First scenario where her own **desk** is named; her union reflex and blame on retail chains and investors are strong.
Resistant but not stubborn: she'd practise the tool with a younger colleague, grudgingly.
Starts to think about leaving at 62, which is a real change from her plan.

steps.text: Join every union meeting and push for no forced redundancies
Practise the ordering tool with Mia on Friday afternoons
Stop the extra 150 a month to my daughter
Work out with Tomas if stopping at 62 is possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody can be ready for two years, and that governments should be on the news tonight explaining what they'll do for people like me. I'd ask the union for a public meeting, and I'd tell my friends this is not a story about gadgets, it's about who eats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job is gone, maybe within 18 months, and I'm 58 with four months saved. Nobody hires a 59-year-old buyer who never touched the tools. Robots come later, but that doesn't help me, because my work is all thinking and phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost I can, stop the help for my daughter, and ask Tomas whether we could live on his council wage and my savings. I'd go to the union and the government office and ask what support exists. I'd also try to get a redundancy package in writing before they finish the restructure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the floor going soft. I'd probably lie awake and run the numbers at 3 in the morning. I'd be frightened, but also furious that this happens to people who did everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd run the numbers at 3 in the morning. What do they look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months of savings, a mortgage with about nine years to go, and Tomas's wage covering maybe half of it. If I get a payout, it stretches to a year. After that we'd sell the car and look at the smaller flat near my sister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter the day you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't count on us for the rent any more, and I'm sorry. Then I'd tell her to get her own training in something with hands, like nursing. I'd rather she was ahead of this than behind it.

say: I'd say **two years** is far too little, and government should explain tonight what it will do for people like me.
I'd ask the union for a **public meeting**.
think: My job is **gone within 18 months**, and nobody hires a 59-year-old buyer.
Robots coming later doesn't help me, because my work is all **thinking and phones**.
do: Cut every cost and **stop helping** my daughter with rent.
Press for a **written redundancy package** before the restructure ends.
Ask the union and government office what **support** exists.
feel: **Frightened** and furious that this happens to people who did everything right.
S2.quote: Nobody hires a 59-year-old buyer who never touched the tools.
fieldNote: Expects to lose her job and money is thin, so this is **alarm** rather than anxiety.
Her blame turns on governments and employers who had no plan; she is practical about selling the car and downsizing.
Turns toward her daughter's future, urging her to train in something hands-on.

steps.text: Stop the monthly rent help to my daughter
Ask the government office what support exists for laid-off workers
Ask the union to secure a written redundancy package
Tell my daughter to train in nursing or another hands-on trade

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's not nothing, so there's room to make sensible rules. I'd tell the union to start talks with the employers now. At home I'd say we should keep our heads and make a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd probably be out before I'm 63, because the thinking work goes at the date and my desk is thinking work. But I might get to 62 with a decent payout if the union wins something. Robots come three years after, so it's my daughter's generation I worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the mortgage as fast as I can, aim for about a year of savings, and ask the union for retraining money. I'd probably do an evening course in something people-facing, like supplier relations or a hospital supplies role. I'd also learn the tools properly, because I'd have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A countdown I can see is better than a surprise. I'm anxious, but I have some control. I'd feel sad about the end of the phone calls and the people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay down the mortgage. What would you drop to make that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The weekend away every month, and the extra helping hand for my daughter. We'd also stop eating out on Fridays. It would be about 500 a month, and I'd put it straight onto the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the evening course be, and who would pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a hospital procurement certificate at the technical college, about 900 for the year. I'd ask the union's training fund first. If they say no, I'd pay myself, because it's the one thing that might get me another job at 59.

say: I'd say **five years** is short but there's room to make sensible rules.
I'd tell the union to start talks with employers **now**.
think: I'll probably be out before **63**, because my desk is thinking work.
Robots come three years later, so it's my **daughter's generation** I worry about.
do: Put about **500 a month** onto the mortgage.
Do an evening **hospital procurement** course at the technical college.
Learn the AI tools properly, because I'd have to.
feel: **Anxious**, but better than a surprise, and sad about losing the phone calls.
S3.quote: A countdown I can see is better than a surprise.
fieldNote: The visible five-year window gives her **control**, which keeps her at anxious rather than alarmed.
Concrete, local plan: technical college course and a union training fund.
Sentimental about her supplier relationships, which she knows are what she will miss.

steps.text: Pay 500 a month extra onto the mortgage
Take a hospital procurement certificate at the technical college
Learn the ordering and invoice tools properly with Mia
Stop the monthly weekend away and Friday meals out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and I'd be glad of it. At the union I'd say it's our chance to get rules and retraining rights written down while there's time. I'd tell my friends I'd be retired by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be out the door of the job by 65 whatever happens, so ten years is mostly about my pension and my daughter. If I last to 62 I'd be fine. The real fear is that my pension is smaller than we thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, finish paying off the house, and retire at 62 or 63. I'd give a few hours a week to the union committee. I'd maybe try the new tools in the last couple of years so I'm not a fossil, but I wouldn't rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels manageable. I'd feel a bit relieved and a bit guilty about being lucky. I'd still be uneasy about the world my daughter walks into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your pension. What would you want to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How much it pays at 62 compared with 65, and whether the employer's part is protected if the company is sold or cut. I'd ask the union to get that in writing. A leaflet saying 'don't worry' isn't enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in the first year if you had ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd tell Tomas I'd like to work till 62, no more. I'd also go for a walk every day, honestly, because after twenty years at a desk my back isn't going to last till 65.

say: I'd say **ten years** is time to get rules and retraining rights written down.
I'd tell friends I'll be **retired by then** anyway.
think: I'd be out of the job by **65** whatever happens, so this is about my pension.
My real fear is a **smaller pension** than we thought.
do: Finish paying off the **house** and aim to retire at 62.
Give a few hours a week to the **union committee**.
Try the **new tools** in the last couple of working years.
feel: **Manageable** and a little guilty about being lucky, still uneasy for my daughter.
S4.quote: A leaflet saying 'don't worry' isn't enough for me.
fieldNote: Ten years sits with her **retirement**, so her own job feels safe enough; the concern shifts to the pension and her daughter.
Guarded about reassurance, needs written guarantees via the union.
Still wary but willing to learn the tools late, on her own terms.

steps.text: Keep buying for the distributor until 62
Pay off the remaining nine years of mortgage early
Join the union committee for a few hours a week
Learn the ordering tools in the final two years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I'd have no time to get anywhere. What would help is a proper safety net: a decent payout, retraining that someone else pays for, and employers having to talk to the union before they bring in anything. And a pension nobody can touch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change. I'm against change that happens to people instead of with them. If someone asked me about the tools properly, with time, I'd probably learn them.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change. I'm against change that happens to people instead of with them.
portrait: Amira, 58, buys disposable packaging for a **food-service distributor** and has known the cup factory rep for twenty years.
Progressive and **union-minded**, she blames big retail chains and investors, not the software itself.
Resistant to new tools, with about **four months** saved and a daughter whose rent she helps with.
She is uneasy in the mild worlds, **alarmed** if AGI arrives in 2 years, and relaxed only when the timeline nears retirement.
Her first move in every scenario is to **go to the union** and ask for things in writing.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, because there would be no time to prepare, and she is 58 with a thin cushion.
whatWouldHelp: A **decent payout**, paid retraining, a union say before changes, and a **protected pension**.
